item.title: Acid–Base Regulation
item.description: Diuretics increase urine output primarily by inhibiting renal tubular sodium reabsorption, causing natriuresis and water loss; different classes act at distinct nephron sites including the loop of Henle, distal tubule, and collecting duct.

item.title: Adrenocortical Hormones
item.description: Insulin, secreted by pancreatic beta cells, is an anabolic hormone that promotes glucose uptake, glycogen synthesis, lipogenesis, and protein synthesis; its deficiency causes diabetes mellitus. Glucagon from alpha cells opposes insulin by stimulating glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, maintaining blood glucose during fasting.

item.title: Autonomic Nervous System and the Adrenal Medulla
item.description: The autonomic nervous system (ANS) consists of sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions that control involuntary functions of visceral organs. Sympathetic neurons originate from spinal cord T1-L2, pass through paravertebral ganglia and prevertebral ganglia to reach effectors. Parasympathetic fibers travel via cranial nerves III, VII, IX, X and sacral nerves S2-S4. The adrenal medulla, embryologically a sympathetic ganglion, secretes epinephrine and norepinephrine directly into the bloodstream.

item.title: Aviation, High Altitude, and Space Physiology
item.description: As altitude increases, barometric pressure falls, causing alveolar PO2 to decline and leading to hypoxia; breathing pure oxygen at high altitude dramatically raises alveolar PO2 by eliminating nitrogen dilution. Acclimatization involves increased ventilation, erythrocytosis, increased diffusing capacity, and enhanced tissue vascularity. Acute hypoxia causes impaired judgment, drowsiness, and seizures above 18,000 feet without acclimatization.

item.title: Blood Types; Transfusion; and Tissue and Organ Transplantation
item.description: Organ transplantation success depends on HLA antigen matching between donor and recipient; autografts and isografts are accepted without immunosuppression, while allografts and xenografts require varying degrees of immune suppression using glucocorticoids, cyclosporine, tacrolimus, or antilymphocyte antibodies.

item.title: Body Temperature Regulation and Fever
item.description: Core body temperature is maintained at ~98.6°F (37°C) by balancing heat production (from metabolism and muscle activity) against heat loss (via radiation, conduction, convection, and evaporation). The hypothalamus serves as the thermoregulatory center, integrating afferent temperature signals and orchestrating autonomic and behavioral responses. Fever results from pyrogen-mediated elevation of the hypothalamic set-point, whereas heat stroke and hypothermia represent failures of thermoregulation.

item.title: Capillary Dynamics and Fluid Exchange
item.description: Fluid exchange across the capillary membrane is governed by Starling forces, which include hydrostatic pressure gradients driving filtration and oncotic pressure gradients opposing it. Osmotic pressure differences between plasma and interstitial fluid are critical for maintaining vascular volume and cellular hydration.

item.title: Cardiac Arrhythmias and Their Electrocardiographic Interpretation
item.description: Cardiac arrhythmias result from abnormalities in impulse formation or conduction within the cardiac conduction system. ECG diagnosis distinguishes sinus node dysfunction (tachycardia, bradycardia, sinus arrhythmia), conduction blocks (SA block, AV block of varying degrees), and circus movement arrhythmias (atrial flutter, atrial fibrillation, ventricular fibrillation).

item.title: Cardiac Failure
item.description: This chapter describes normal heart sounds and their physiologic origins, detailing the first heart sound (S1) from A-V valve closure, the second heart sound (S2) from semilunar valve closure, the third heart sound (S3) in early diastole, and the fourth heart sound (S4) associated with atrial contraction. It also covers auscultation sites, phonocardiography, and how valvular heart disease produces abnormal murmurs.

item.title: Cardiac Muscle: The Heart as a Pump and Function of the Heart Valves
item.description: The heart functions as two sequential pumps—right and left heart—each with an atrium and ventricle, separated into atrial and ventricular syncytiums by the fibrous A-V ring. Cardiac muscle has a prolonged plateau action potential (~0.2s) due to L-type Ca2+ channels, which prevents tetanic contraction and allows efficient pumping.

item.title: Cardiac Output, Venous Return, and Their Regulation
item.description: Cardiac output equals venous return and is normally regulated by the sum of all local tissue blood flows via the Frank-Starling mechanism. The heart automatically pumps whatever volume returns from the veins; long-term cardiac output varies inversely with total peripheral resistance when arterial pressure is held constant.

item.title: Cerebellum and Basal Ganglia Contributions to Overall Motor Control
item.description: The cerebellum and basal ganglia are essential for normal motor function, operating in association with cortical and brain stem motor control systems. The cerebellum coordinates timing and smooth progression between sequential muscle movements, compares intended movements with actual feedback, and makes real-time corrective adjustments. The basal ganglia help plan complex motor patterns and control parallel and sequential movements required for purposeful tasks.

item.title: Cerebral Blood Flow, Cerebrospinal Fluid, and Brain Metabolism
item.description: The brain has high metabolic demands but limited energy storage, requiring continuous delivery of glucose and oxygen from blood. Cerebral blood flow is tightly regulated by metabolic, autoregulatory, and neurogenic mechanisms. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) is produced by choroid plexus and circulates through ventricles and subarachnoid space, providing mechanical protection and waste removal. The blood-brain barrier protects neural tissue from harmful substances.

item.title: Cerebral Cortex, Intellectual Functions of the Brain, Learning, and Memory
item.description: The cerebral cortex is organized into six histological layers containing granular, pyramidal, and fusiform neurons that process sensory information and generate motor commands. Different cortical areas have specific functions: primary motor cortex controls discrete muscle movements, premotor and supplementary motor areas plan complex patterns, and association areas integrate multimodal information for higher cognitive functions including learning and memory.

item.title: Circulatory Shock and Its Treatment
item.description: This chapter covers the pathophysiology of circulatory shock, including its classification into hypovolemic, cardiogenic, and distributive types. It details the compensatory mechanisms activated during hemorrhage, the progressive stages of shock leading to tissue deterioration, and the physiologic basis of treatment approaches including fluid resuscitation, sympathomimetic drugs, and management of circulatory arrest.

item.title: Contraction of Skeletal Muscle
item.description: Skeletal muscle contraction occurs through the sliding filament mechanism, where actin filaments slide over myosin filaments powered by ATP hydrolysis. The sarcomere is the basic contractile unit, delimited by Z disks, with A bands and I bands reflecting the overlap of thick and thin filaments.

item.title: Dietary Balances; Regulation of Feeding; Obesity and Starvation; Vitamins and Minerals
item.description: Energy balance requires caloric intake equal to expenditure; excess energy is stored primarily as fat. Food intake is regulated by hypothalamic hunger/satiety centers responding to metabolic signals (leptin, ghrelin, insulin, glucose) and GI hormones. Starvation triggers glycogen depletion, protein catabolism, and ketogenesis. Vitamins are essential organic cofactors, and minerals serve structural, enzymatic, and electrochemical functions. The respiratory quotient (RQ = CO₂/O₂) reflects the mix of macronutrients oxidized.

item.title: Digestion and Absorption in the Gastrointestinal Tract
item.description: Digestion breaks down carbohydrates, fats, and proteins into absorbable units through hydrolysis reactions catalyzed by specific enzymes from saliva, gastric juice, pancreatic juice, and intestinal brush border enzymes. Carbohydrates are ultimately digested to monosaccharides (80% glucose), fats to fatty acids and monoglycerides, and proteins to amino acids. Absorption occurs primarily in the small intestine via active transport and facilitated diffusion, with the large intestine absorbing water, electrolytes, and forming feces.

item.title: Diuretics and Kidney Diseases
item.description: Red blood cells (RBCs) are biconcave discs that transport hemoglobin and facilitate CO2 transport via carbonic anhydrase; they are produced from hematopoietic stem cells in bone marrow and regulated by erythropoietin.

item.title: Electrocardiographic Interpretation of Cardiac Muscle and Coronary Blood Flow Abnormalities
item.description: T wave abnormalities on ECG reflect altered repolarization sequences caused by conditions such as ischemia, bundle branch block, or digitalis toxicity. The polarity and morphology of the T wave provide diagnostic clues about the underlying cardiac pathology affecting ventricular repolarization.

item.title: Energetics and Metabolic Rate
item.description: ATP serves as the universal energy currency coupling energy-producing oxidative metabolism of foodstuffs to energy-consuming cellular work including muscle contraction, active transport, synthesis, and nerve conduction. Phosphocreatine functions as an ATP buffer, rapidly regenerating ATP from ADP. Metabolic rate is measured by direct or indirect calorimetry and is increased by physical activity, hormone effects (thyroxine, catecholamines), thermic effect of food, and temperature. Anaerobic glycolysis provides rapid energy during hypoxia and brief strenuous activity.

item.title: Excitation and Contraction of Smooth Muscle
item.description: Smooth muscle contracts using actin-myosin interaction similar to skeletal muscle but lacks troponin, relying instead on Ca2+-calmodulin and myosin light chain kinase for regulation. Unitary smooth muscle forms syncytial networks with gap junctions, while multi-unit smooth muscle operates independently with discrete innervation.

item.title: Excitation of Skeletal Muscle: Neuromuscular Transmission and Excitation-Contraction Coupling
item.description: Neuromuscular transmission occurs at the motor end plate where acetylcholine is released from nerve terminals, binding to nicotinic receptors and causing depolarization. Excitation-contraction coupling links this depolarization to Ca2+ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, activating cross-bridge cycling through the DHP and ryanodine receptors.

item.title: Female Physiology Before Pregnancy and Female Hormones
item.description: The female monthly sexual cycle involves coordinated hypothalamic GnRH pulses, anterior pituitary FSH/LH secretion, and ovarian estrogen/progesterone production, culminating in ovulation and preparation of the uterus for potential pregnancy. Oogenesis produces a single mature ovum per cycle from primordial follicles.

item.title: Fetal and Neonatal Physiology
item.description: The transition from fetal to neonatal life requires dramatic physiological changes, particularly in respiratory, circulatory, and metabolic systems. Premature infants face significant challenges due to organ immaturity, including respiratory distress syndrome, poor GI absorption, liver dysfunction, and unstable homeostatic control.

item.title: Functional Organization of the Human Body and Control of the Internal Environment
item.description: The human body consists of cells organized into tissues, organs, and organ systems that work together to maintain homeostasis. Cells are composed of protoplasm containing water, electrolytes, proteins, lipids, and carbohydrates, with organelles performing specialized functions.

item.title: Fundamentals of Electrocardiography
item.description: The ECG records the summation of cardiac electrical potentials as vectors during depolarization and repolarization. Vectorial analysis allows interpretation of the ECG waveform in different leads by projecting the instantaneous mean vector onto each lead axis, enabling localization of cardiac electrical activity.

item.title: General Principles of Gastrointestinal Function—Motility, Nervous Control, and Blood Circulation
item.description: The gastrointestinal tract propels, mixes, and absorbs food through coordinated smooth muscle contractions controlled by enteric nervous system, autonomic nerves, and hormones. Gastrointestinal smooth muscle exhibits spontaneous electrical slow waves and spike potentials that determine contraction rhythms. Blood flow to GI organs is regulated by metabolic demands and sympathetic/parasympathetic nervous system activity.

item.title: Genetic Control of Protein Synthesis, Cell Function, and Cell Reproduction
item.description: Genes are DNA sequences that control cell function by directing protein synthesis through transcription of DNA to mRNA and subsequent translation at ribosomes. The genome contains the complete blueprint for cellular structure, enzyme production, and cell reproduction.

item.title: Glomerular Filtration, Renal Blood Flow, and Their Control
item.description: This chapter covers the determinants and regulation of glomerular filtration rate (GFR) and renal blood flow (RBF), including the Starling forces governing filtration across the glomerular capillaries, autoregulation mechanisms (myogenic and tubuloglomerular feedback), and factors that alter RBF and GFR such as diet, metabolic states, and aging. It also describes the measurement of GFR using inulin clearance and RBF using PAH clearance.

item.title: Heart Valves and Heart Sounds; Valvular and Congenital Heart Defects
item.description: This chapter covers cardiac failure, including the acute compensatory responses via sympathetic nervous system activation and the chronic stage involving fluid retention. Acute myocardial infarction causes immediate depression of cardiac output and rise in venous pressure, triggering reflexes that partially restore circulation. Prolonged cardiac failure leads to renal fluid retention that can be initially beneficial but eventually detrimental, causing pulmonary edema and peripheral congestion.

item.title: Hemostasis and Blood Coagulation
item.description: Hemostasis prevents blood loss through vascular constriction, platelet plug formation, and fibrin clot formation; the intrinsic and extrinsic coagulation pathways converge on the common pathway leading to thrombin generation and fibrin mesh formation.

item.title: Insulin, Glucagon, and Diabetes Mellitus
item.description: Plasma calcium exists as ionized (50%), protein-bound (41%), and complexed (9%) fractions; precise regulation of ionized calcium (~1.2 mmol/L) is critical for neuromuscular excitability, muscle contraction, and blood clotting. Hypocalcemia causes tetany and seizures, while hypercalcemia depresses the nervous system and can lead to calcium phosphate precipitation.

item.title: Introduction to Endocrinology
item.description: The pituitary gland, composed of anterior (adenohypophysis) and posterior (neurohypophysis) lobes, secretes nine major peptide hormones that regulate metabolism, growth, reproduction, water balance, and lactation throughout the body.

item.title: Lipid Metabolism
item.description: Triglycerides are the primary storage form of dietary fat and are transported from the intestines as chylomicrons via lymphatic vessels. Fatty acids serve as a major energy source during fasting, transported in blood bound to albumin as free fatty acids. Lipoprotein lipase hydrolyzes chylomicron triglycerides in capillary beds, and the liver clears cholesterol-rich chylomicron remnants. Beta-oxidation of fatty acids in mitochondria generates acetyl-CoA for the citric acid cycle, while excess acetyl-CoA is converted to ketone bodies during prolonged fasting.

item.title: Local and Humoral Control of Tissue Blood Flow
item.description: Tissue blood flow is regulated by local metabolic factors and circulating hormones that act directly on vascular smooth muscle. Chemical factors including ions (K+, Ca2+, Mg2+, H+), CO2, and adenosine cause vasodilation, while autoregulation maintains constant flow despite pressure changes. Long-term blood flow is ultimately determined by tissue metabolic needs.

item.title: Membrane Potentials and Action Potentials
item.description: Membrane potentials arise from ion concentration gradients across selectively permeable membranes. Resting membrane potential is determined primarily by potassium conductance, while action potentials result from rapid, sequential changes in sodium and potassium permeability during depolarization and repolarization.

item.title: Metabolism of Carbohydrates and Formation of Adenosine Triphosphate
item.description: Glucose is the central carbohydrate for metabolism, converted from dietary carbohydrates in the liver, and serves as the primary energy substrate for most tissues. ATP functions as the universal energy currency of the body, generated through glycolysis (anaerobic) and mitochondrial oxidative metabolism (aerobic). The complete oxidation of glucose through glycolysis, pyruvate decarboxylation, the citric acid cycle, and oxidative phosphorylation yields approximately 30-32 ATP molecules per molecule of glucose.

item.title: Muscle Blood Flow and Cardiac Output During Exercise
item.description: This chapter covers cardiac failure, including the acute compensatory responses via sympathetic nervous system activation and the chronic stage involving fluid retention. Acute myocardial infarction causes immediate depression of cardiac output and rise in venous pressure, triggering reflexes that partially restore circulation. Prolonged cardiac failure leads to renal fluid retention that can be initially beneficial but eventually detrimental, causing pulmonary edema and peripheral congestion.

item.title: Nervous Regulation of the Circulation and Rapid Control of Arterial Pressure
item.description: The autonomic nervous system provides rapid, global control of circulation through sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions. Sympathetic stimulation increases heart rate, contractility, and vasoconstriction (especially in veins and resistance vessels of kidneys, intestines, spleen, and skin), while parasympathetic vagal stimulation slows heart rate via the sinoatrial node.

item.title: Organization of the Nervous System, Basic Functions of Synapses, and Neurotransmitters
item.description: The nervous system is organized into sensory, integrative, and motor divisions that process information from receptors to effectors. Synapses are the functional junctions between neurons where signal transmission is modulated by excitatory or inhibitory neurotransmitters and affected by synaptic fatigue and receptor regulation. The brain processes only salient sensory information, filtering out 99% of incoming data as irrelevant through selective synaptic transmission.

item.title: Overview of the Circulation: Pressure, Flow, and Resistance
item.description: The circulation consists of systemic and pulmonary circuits with distinct functions: arteries transport high-pressure blood, arterioles control flow resistance, capillaries permit fluid exchange, and veins serve as a blood reservoir. Blood flow velocity is inversely proportional to cross-sectional area, and mean aortic pressure (100 mm Hg) is maintained by cardiac output against total peripheral resistance.

item.title: Parathyroid Hormone, Calcitonin, Calcium and Phosphate Metabolism, Vitamin D, Bone, and Teeth
item.description: Spermatogenesis occurs in the seminiferous tubules of the testes under gonadotropic hormone control, producing mature spermatozoa through mitotic proliferation, meiotic division, and differentiation over approximately 74 days. Leydig cells secrete testosterone, which together with FSH acting on Sertoli cells, regulates spermatogenesis.

item.title: Physiology of Deep-Sea Diving and Other Hyperbaric Conditions
item.description: Under hyperbaric conditions, increased nitrogen pressure causes nitrogen narcosis (raptures of the depths) similar to alcohol intoxication, while oxygen toxicity and CO2 retention become significant hazards. Decompression sickness results from bubble formation during ascent when dissolved nitrogen comes out of solution. Open-circuit SCUBA systems deliver compressed air on demand, while hyperbaric oxygen therapy uses 2-3 atm O2 to treat conditions like gas gangrene, CO poisoning, and decompression sickness.

item.title: Physiology of Gastrointestinal Disorders
item.description: This chapter reviews gastrointestinal pathology including peptic ulcer disease, Helicobacter pylori infection, pancreatitis, gallbladder disease, malabsorption syndromes, inflammatory bowel disease, and functional gastrointestinal disorders. Understanding the underlying physiology of these disorders is essential for rational diagnosis and treatment.

item.title: Pituitary Hormones and Their Control by the Hypothalamus
item.description: The hypothalamus controls the posterior pituitary via neural pathways (releasing ADH and oxytocin from magnocellular neurons) and regulates the anterior pituitary through portal vein delivery of releasing/inhibiting hormones. ADH secretion is primarily controlled by plasma osmolarity via osmoreceptors and by blood volume/pressure via baroreceptors.

item.title: Pregnancy and Lactation
item.description: Following ovulation, the secondary oocyte is captured by the fimbriated end of the fallopian tube and transported to the ampulla where fertilization typically occurs. Sperm capacitation, the acrosome reaction, and fusion of male and female pronuclei are essential steps in successful fertilization.

item.title: Principles of Gas Exchange; Diffusion of Oxygen and Carbon Dioxide Through the Respiratory Membrane
item.description: Gas diffusion between alveoli and blood is driven by partial pressure gradients; oxygenation of pulmonary capillary blood occurs rapidly (within the first third of capillary length), and blood serves as a carrier for O2 (as oxyhemoglobin) and CO2 (as bicarbonate), with tissue metabolism creating gradients that drive gas exchange.

item.title: Propulsion and Mixing of Food in the Alimentary Tract
item.description: Food propulsion and mixing in the GI tract involve coordinated motor patterns including peristalsis, segmentation, and mass movements. Swallowing is a complex reflex with voluntary oral phase and involuntary pharyngeal/esophageal phases controlled by the swallowing center in the medulla. The enteric nervous system coordinates local GI motility, while autonomic reflexes and central programs regulate overall gut motor activity.

item.title: Protein Metabolism
item.description: Dietary proteins are digested to amino acids and absorbed; amino acid concentration in blood is tightly regulated at 35-65 mg/dL. The liver is the primary site of amino acid metabolism, where transamination and oxidative deamination remove nitrogen for urea synthesis. Deaminated amino acids enter the citric acid cycle for energy or are used for gluconeogenesis and ketogenesis. Protein turnover is continuous, with 20-30 g/day obligatory degradation requiring dietary protein replacement.

item.title: Pulmonary Circulation, Pulmonary Edema, and Pleural Fluid
item.description: The pleural space is a potential space with negative pressure (~-7 mm Hg) maintained by lymphatic drainage; pulmonary edema develops when capillary hydrostatic pressure exceeds plasma colloid osmotic pressure, and pleural effusion results from similar Starling forces plus inflammation.

item.title: Pulmonary Ventilation
item.description: The pulmonary circulation has low pressures (mean pulmonary artery pressure ~15 mm Hg) compared to the systemic circulation; pulmonary capillary pressure (~7 mm Hg) is kept low to prevent pulmonary edema, and the lungs serve as a blood reservoir that can shift blood to systemic circulation.

item.title: Red Blood Cells, Anemia, and Polycythemia
item.description: Polycythemia refers to an elevated RBC count and can be secondary to tissue hypoxia (e.g., high altitude) or primary (polycythemia vera); it increases blood viscosity, which may impair venous return and cause cyanosis.

item.title: Regulation of Body Fluid Compartments: Extracellular and Intracellular Fluids; Edema
item.description: This chapter describes the regulation of body fluid compartments, including the distribution of total body water between intracellular (28L) and extracellular (14L) compartments in a 70kg adult, and the mechanisms controlling fluid intake and output. It details how insensible water loss, sweat, feces, and urine contribute to daily water balance, and how the kidneys adjust urine output from 0.5 to 20 L/day to match variable intake.

item.title: Regulation of Respiration
item.description: Respiration is regulated by the brainstem respiratory center, which generates automatic rhythmic breathing through the dorsal inspiratory group and ventral expiratory group of neurons. Chemical feedback from peripheral and central chemoreceptors adjusts ventilation to maintain blood O2, CO2, and pH within narrow limits. Higher cortical centers allow voluntary control of breathing, while lung stretch receptors provide a protective reflex that limits inspiration.

item.title: Renal Regulation of Potassium, Calcium, Phosphate, and Magnesium
item.description: This chapter covers the renal regulation of potassium, calcium, phosphate, and magnesium, with emphasis on the precise control of extracellular potassium concentration. It describes how potassium distribution between intracellular and extracellular compartments is regulated by insulin, aldosterone, β-adrenergic stimulation, acid-base status, and cell lysis, and how the kidneys control potassium excretion through filtration, reabsorption, and secretion.

item.title: Renal Tubular Reabsorption and Secretion
item.description: This chapter details the mechanisms of tubular reabsorption and secretion, explaining how the kidneys reabsorb more than 99% of the filtered water and solutes while selectively excreting waste products. It covers primary and secondary active transport, passive diffusion, and osmosis as transport mechanisms, and describes how substances can move via transcellular or paracellular pathways across the tubular epithelium.

item.title: Reproductive and Hormonal Functions of the Male (and Function of the Pineal Gland)
item.description: Spermatogenesis occurs in the seminiferous tubules of the testes under gonadotropic hormone control, producing mature spermatozoa through mitotic proliferation, meiotic division, and differentiation over approximately 74 days. Leydig cells secrete testosterone, which together with FSH acting on Sertoli cells, regulates spermatogenesis.

item.title: Resistance of the Body to Infection
item.description: Basophils and mast cells mediate allergic inflammation by releasing histamine, heparin, and other mediators; leukopenia leaves the body vulnerable to infection, while leukemia is uncontrolled proliferation of WBCs causing organ infiltration and metabolic exhaustion.

item.title: Resistance of the Body to Infection: II. Immunity and Allergy
item.description: Acquired immunity involves B-cell (humoral) and T-cell (cell-mediated) responses directed against specific antigens; T cells are thymus-processed and B cells are bone marrow-processed; allergy represents hypersensitivity mediated by IgE and mast cell degranulation or by sensitized T cells.

item.title: Respiratory Insufficiency—Pathophysiology, Diagnosis, Oxygen Therapy
item.description: Respiratory insufficiency encompasses abnormalities in maximum expiratory flow-volume curves, used to diagnose obstructive and restrictive lung diseases. The flow-volume relationship reveals how airway resistance, lung compliance, and respiratory muscle strength determine ventilatory capacity.

item.title: Rhythmical Excitation of the Heart
item.description: The sinoatrial (SA) node is the primary pacemaker of the heart, generating spontaneous action potentials through funny current (If) mediated by high membrane leakiness to Na+ and Ca2+. The action potential spreads through internodal pathways to the AV node (where it delays), then through the His-Purkinje system to ventricular muscle.

item.title: Role of the Kidneys in Long-Term Control of Arterial Pressure and in Hypertension
item.description: The renal-body fluid system is the primary mechanism for long-term arterial pressure control through pressure diuresis and pressure natriuresis. The equilibrium point where renal fluid output equals intake determines the steady-state arterial pressure; this point can be shifted by kidney function changes or salt intake, forming the basis of hypertension.

item.title: Secretory Functions of the Alimentary Tract
item.description: The gastrointestinal tract secretes digestive enzymes, mucus, and electrolytes through highly regulated mechanisms involving neural, hormonal, and paracrine controls. Salivary, gastric, pancreatic, biliary, and intestinal secretions work sequentially to break down food, while the large intestine primarily secretes protective mucus. Enteric nervous system reflexes triggered by chyme are the principal regulators of small intestine secretion.

item.title: Sensory Receptors, Neuronal Circuits for Processing Information
item.description: Sensory receptors transduce specific stimuli into electrical signals via receptor potentials, following the labeled line principle where each fiber transmits only one sensation type. The five receptor classes are mechanoreceptors, thermoreceptors, nociceptors, electromagnetic receptors, and chemoreceptors. Neuronal circuits use excitatory and inhibitory pathways with reverberating circuits for signal amplification and synaptic fatigue for short-term sensitivity regulation.

item.title: Somatic Sensations: I. General Organization, Tactile and Position Senses
item.description: Somatic sensations include tactile (touch, pressure, vibration) and proprioceptive (position, movement) senses mediated by specialized mechanoreceptors in skin and deep tissues. Different receptor types adapt at different rates to encode stimulus intensity and duration; Pacinian corpuscles detect rapid vibration (30-800 Hz) while Ruffini endings signal sustained pressure. Tactile signals are transmitted via large-diameter Aβ myelinated fibers for precise localization, and smaller Aδ or C fibers for crude touch and tickle.

item.title: Somatic Sensations: II. Pain and Temperature
item.description: Pain and temperature sensations are detected by specialized receptors (nociceptors and thermoreceptors) and transmitted via specific sensory pathways to the brain. The hypothalamus serves as the central integrator for temperature regulation, coordinating vasomotor, sweating, and shivering responses to maintain thermal homeostasis.

item.title: Spinal Cord Motor Functions; the Cord Reflexes
item.description: The spinal cord contains the neuronal circuitry essential for all motor control, including reflex arcs that operate independently of brain input. Sensory signals enter through dorsal roots and synapse on interneurons or directly on anterior motor neurons (alpha and gamma types), which innervate skeletal muscle fibers. Propriospinal fibers coordinate multisegmental movements, while Renshaw cells provide lateral inhibition to sharpen motor output.

item.title: Sports Physiology
item.description: Sports physiology examines the acute responses and long-term adaptations of cardiovascular, respiratory, muscular, and metabolic systems to exercise. Both anaerobic (strength/sprint) and aerobic (endurance) training produce distinct physiological adaptations that enhance athletic performance.

item.title: States of Brain Activity—Sleep, Brain Waves, Epilepsy, Psychoses, and Dementia
item.description: Brain activity cycles between wakefulness, REM sleep, and non-REM (slow-wave) sleep, each with distinct EEG patterns and physiological characteristics. Sleep is actively induced by inhibitory centers in the brain stem and hypothalamus, particularly serotonergic neurons in the raphe nuclei. Various neurological conditions including epilepsy, psychoses, and dementia involve specific patterns of brain activity disruption.

item.title: The Cell and Its Functions
item.description: Cells contain specialized organelles enclosed by membranes that perform distinct functions essential for cell survival. The nucleus houses DNA and controls cell activities, while the cytoplasm contains the machinery for energy production, protein synthesis, and intracellular transport.

item.title: The Chemical Senses—Taste and Smell
item.description: The chemical senses of taste and smell enable detection of chemical molecules in the environment. Olfaction is mediated through olfactory bulb glomeruli where odorant receptors converge, with three parallel pathways (primitive medial, less old lateral, and newer thalamic) providing basic reflexes, food intake control, and conscious perception. Taste involves five primary qualities detected by gustatory receptor cells, transmitting signals via cranial nerves VII, IX, and X to the brain stem and thalamus.

item.title: The Limbic System and the Hypothalamus—Behavioral and Motivational Mechanisms of the Brain
item.description: The limbic system and hypothalamus form the brain’s motivational and behavioral control center, working with brain stem reticular activating system to regulate arousal, sleep-wake cycles, and motivated behaviors. The hypothalamus maintains homeostasis by controlling autonomic function, endocrine secretion, thirst, hunger, and temperature regulation. Neurohormonal systems using serotonin, norepinephrine, dopamine, and acetylcholine modulate brain activity and behavior.

item.title: The Liver
item.description: The liver is the largest organ in the body, performing over 500 functions including metabolism of carbohydrates, proteins, and fats; formation and secretion of bile; detoxification of hormones, drugs, and toxins; synthesis of plasma proteins and clotting factors; and storage of vitamins and iron. The liver lobule is the functional unit, with hepatocytes arranged in plates between sinusoidal capillaries, receiving dual blood supply from the portal vein and hepatic artery.

item.title: The Sense of Hearing
item.description: Note: This file contains content from Chapter 54 (Taste and Smell) rather than Chapter 53. Taste is detected by taste buds on the tongue and palate, with five primary modalities (sour, salty, sweet, bitter, umami). Taste thresholds vary widely between modalities, with bitter being most sensitive.

item.title: The Urinary System: Functional Anatomy and Urine Formation by the Kidneys
item.description: This chapter provides an overview of the kidney’s multiple homeostatic functions beyond waste excretion, including regulation of fluid balance, electrolyte composition, arterial pressure, acid-base balance, erythrocyte production, vitamin D activation, and gluconeogenesis. It describes the gross and microscopic anatomy of the kidneys and introduces the three fundamental renal processes: glomerular filtration, tubular reabsorption, and tubular secretion, which together determine urinary excretion rates.

item.title: Thyroid Metabolic Hormones
item.description: The thyroid gland secretes thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3), which regulate basal metabolic rate, growth, and development through genomic mechanisms involving nuclear receptors and mitochondrial effects.

item.title: Transport of Oxygen and Carbon Dioxide in Blood and Tissue Fluids
item.description: Oxygen is transported primarily bound to hemoglobin, with only a small fraction dissolved in plasma, while CO2 is carried as bicarbonate, dissolved gas, and carbaminohemoglobin. The Haldane effect (oxygenation releases CO2) and Bohr effect (CO2 lowers hemoglobin’s O2 affinity) coordinate efficient gas exchange between lungs and tissues. The respiratory exchange ratio (R ≈ 0.825) reflects the balance between O2 uptake and CO2 release under normal metabolic conditions.

item.title: Transport of Substances Through Cell Membranes
item.description: Substances cross cell membranes through diffusion (passive) or active transport (energy-dependent). The cell membrane is a lipid bilayer with channel and carrier proteins that determine selective permeability. Diffusion includes simple diffusion through lipids or pores, and facilitated diffusion via carrier proteins.

item.title: Urine Concentration and Dilution
item.description: This chapter explains how the kidneys form dilute or concentrated urine by precisely regulating water excretion independent of solute excretion. It describes the role of antidiuretic hormone (ADH) in controlling water permeability of the distal tubule and collecting ducts, the countercurrent multiplication system that creates the medullary osmotic gradient, and the mechanisms by which the loop of Henle, distal tubule, and collecting duct each contribute to urine concentration or dilution.

item.title: Vascular Distensibility and Functions of the Arterial and Venous Systems
item.description: Vascular compliance and distensibility determine how blood volume changes affect pressure in different circulatory segments. Veins are 8× more distensible than arteries and serve as the primary blood reservoir; arterial compliance dampens pulsations to produce steady capillary flow. Delayed compliance (stress-relaxation) allows vessels to gradually adjust to volume changes.
